notes.text: For more than 8, you'll need a very big pot, at least 8 quarts. Or make it in two pots side by side.

move.title: Small cubes, one big pot
move.body: Dicing means cutting food into small cubes that are all about the same size. Today you'll dice onion, carrots, celery, and zucchini, soften them in olive oil, and simmer them with tomatoes, beans, and little pasta into minestrone, a hearty Italian soup.

why.title: Planks, sticks, cubes
why.body: Every dice works the same way. Cut flat planks, cut the planks into sticks, then cut across the sticks. Each cut across a row of sticks makes a whole row of cubes, and if the planks and sticks were even, the cubes are too.

why.title: Hard vegetables, smaller cubes
why.body: A carrot is much harder than an onion and takes longer to soften. Cut carrots a little smaller than everything else, and they finish cooking at the same time as the rest.

why.title: The flavor starts in the oil
why.body: Onion, carrot, and celery cooked slowly in olive oil turn soft and sweet before any liquid goes in. Italian cooks call this mix soffritto. It's the base of the whole soup, so give it time.

why.title: Pasta keeps drinking
why.body: Pasta soaks up liquid as it cooks, and it doesn't stop when the stove goes off. That's why it goes in near the end, and why leftover minestrone is thick the next day. Stir in a splash of water when you warm it up.

wrong.sign: The carrots are still hard when everything else is soft
wrong.fix: Keep simmering a few more minutes, and add the pasta only once a carrot squashes easily against the side of the pot.

wrong.sign: The pasta is stuck to the bottom of the pot
wrong.fix: Scrape it loose with the wooden spoon, turn the heat down a little, and stir more often.
Stir in a little water or broth until it's how you like it.
Stir in a pinch more salt, then taste again. Parmesan on top adds salt too.

quiz.q: Why are the carrots cut a little smaller than the onion?
choices: They're harder, so smaller pieces catch up
To fit more on the spoon
quiz.explain: Hard vegetables cook slower, so smaller cubes finish at the same time.

quiz.q: Why does the pasta go in near the end?
choices: It's the last thing you chop
quiz.explain: Pasta drinks up the soup as it cooks, so it goes in last.

substitutions.note: Gluten-free pasta gets soft faster. Start checking it a few minutes early.

steps.text: Rinse the carrots, celery, and zucchini and dry them.

Cut the onion in half through the root and peel it, leaving the root on. Lay each half flat side down, cut strips toward the root without cutting through it, then cut across the strips to dice it. Put it in the large bowl.
steps.tip: The root holds the layers together while you cut.

steps.text: Peel the carrots and cut them into pieces about 3 inches long. Slice a thin strip off one side of each piece so it sits flat. Cut it into thin planks, cut the planks into thin sticks, then cut across the sticks to dice it into small cubes. Add them to the bowl.
steps.tip: Peel away from your hand, and keep your fingers behind the blade.

steps.text: Cut the ends off the celery. Cut each rib into 3-inch pieces, cut them the long way into sticks, then cut across the sticks to dice them. Add them to the bowl.
steps.tip: Hold the food with your hand shaped like a claw: fingertips tucked under, knuckles in front.

steps.text: Cut the ends off the zucchini. Cut it in half the long way, lay it flat side down, cut it into sticks, then dice it. Keep the zucchini on the cutting board, apart from the other vegetables. It goes in later.
Peel the garlic and mince it into tiny bits. Put it in the small bowl.
Open the cans of beans with the can opener. Pour the beans into the colander and rinse them under cold water until the bubbles are gone.
steps.tip: The liquid in the can is salty and gloopy. Rinsing it off keeps the soup clear.

steps.text: Heat the olive oil in the pot over medium heat. Add the onion, carrots, celery, and {qty:salt} salt. Cook, stirring now and then, until the onion is soft and see-through.
steps.look: The onion is soft and clear, and nothing is browning.

steps.text: Add the garlic, thyme, oregano, and pepper. Stir for about a minute, until you can smell the garlic.
steps.tip: Garlic burns fast. As soon as it smells good, move on.

steps.text: Pour in the crushed tomatoes, the broth, and the water. Add the beans. Turn the heat up to high, put the lid on, and bring it to a boil.
steps.tip: Pour slowly, close to the pot, so nothing splashes.

steps.text: Turn the heat down so the soup simmers, and leave the lid off.
steps.look: Small, lazy bubbles, and a carrot cube squashes against the side of the pot.

steps.text: Add the zucchini and the pasta. Keep simmering, stirring every couple of minutes so the pasta doesn't stick to the bottom, until the pasta is tender.
steps.tip: Check the pasta box for its cooking time, and taste a piece when the timer rings. Let it cool on the spoon first.

steps.text: Turn off the stove. Taste the soup on a clean spoon, after letting it cool, and add a pinch more salt if it needs it.
Ladle the soup into bowls and sprinkle parmesan on top if you're using it.
steps.tip: Fill bowls on the counter next to the stove, not over the burner.
